History

The ash catcher is a recent addition to bong design, because it answers a cleaning problem that only appears once a bong is used often: ash and loose material travel down the downstem and foul the main water chamber, so the whole piece needs cleaning after every few sessions. The first ash catchers were separate glass chambers that sat between the bowl and the bong, and the ash-catcher bowl folds the two parts into one piece by building the bowl into the top of the catcher chamber. The combined form spread through smoke shops in the 2010s as borosilicate glassblowing made the extra chamber cheap to produce, and it is now sold in 14 mm and 18 mm joints at 45 and 90 degree angles to match beaker and straight-tube bongs. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The ash-catcher bowl works by putting a small chamber between the bowl and the bong, so ash and coarse debris fall into the chamber instead of entering the main water. It is made from borosilicate glass, with a built-in flower bowl on top and an 18 mm male joint at 90 degrees below, and a common example has a bowl about 22 mm across and 18 mm deep, above a catcher chamber about 34 mm across that holds about 13.6 millilitres of water at a 60 percent fill. Smoke passes from the bowl down through the chamber, where the water and the chamber walls catch ash, and then into the bong. The dry form of the same piece uses no water at all and catches ash in the dry chamber. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature borosilicate glass with a coloured trap band; built-in flower bowl fused to the catcher chamber; no metal or plastic in the smoke path

Dimensions: Bowl 22 mm across and 18 mm deep; catcher chamber 34 mm across, water depth 25 mm; lower joint 18 mm male at 90 degrees

Mechanism: Smoke passes from the deeper Signature bowl into the wider chamber, where it slows and ash falls out into the water; the cleaned smoke continues into the bong

Use: Match the joint size and angle to the bong, add water to about 60 percent of the chamber if wet, pack the built-in bowl, light while drawing gently, empty the catcher after the session

Care: Empty the catcher after each session; rinse with warm water and soak in isopropyl alcohol when resin builds up; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped

Variants: 14 mm and 18 mm joints; 45 and 90 degree angles; wet and dry forms; percless, inline-perc, and honeycomb chambers; coloured trap-band finishes

Materials and design

The ash-catcher bowl is a glass-design choice, and the material is borosilicate glass throughout, chosen because it is heat resistant, chemically inert, and transparent enough that the user can see the ash collecting in the chamber. The wall is about 2 mm thick, which is the working compromise: thinner walls cool faster and are lighter but break more easily, thicker walls survive drops better but add weight at the joint and slow the cooling of the smoke.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine home build for an ash-catcher bowl, and this record says so plainly: fusing a bowl into a glass chamber needs a glassblowing torch, an annealing kiln, and a trained hand, and glassblowing is a skilled trade, not a home craft. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling and fitting a bought catcher, and it works like this.

3D printing

The ash-catcher bowl itself is not 3D-printable in glass on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives the heat at the bowl end, so a printed catcher would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG upright stand that cradles the catcher chamber and keeps it from rolling off a table.

Use and program

To use the ash-catcher bowl, match the joint to the bong, 18 mm to 18 mm, and the angle to the bong, 90 degrees for a straight tube and 45 degrees for a beaker. If it is a wet catcher, add water to about 60 percent of the chamber and no higher.

Science proof

An ash catcher works by gravity and by impaction, two pieces of physics that need no electronics. Ash particles leaving the bowl are heavier than smoke, so when the smoke stream turns and slows in the wider catcher chamber, the ash falls out of the stream and lands in the water or on the chamber floor, while the gas keeps moving. The chamber cross-section is about 908 square millimetres, far wider than the 18 mm joint, so the smoke slows by roughly the ratio of the areas and the particles have time to drop. Water in a wet catcher adds a second trap: particles that reach the water surface are wetted and stay there instead of bouncing back into the stream. Borosilicate glass matters because it has a low coefficient of thermal expansion, about 3.3 times ten to the minus six per kelvin, so it tolerates the hot bowl end and the cool joint without cracking, and because glass is chemically inert it adds no flavour of its own. The bowl is a shallow cylinder, so its volume is pi times radius squared times depth, and the chamber is a wider cylinder whose water volume is its fill fraction times its full volume. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports.

Math proof

The demo treats the bowl and the catcher chamber as cylinders. With a bowl diameter of 22.0 mm and a depth of 18.0 mm, the radius is 11.0 mm, so the bowl volume is pi times 121 times 18, about 6,842 cubic millimetres, or 6.84 cubic centimetres. At the stated packing density of 0.15 grams per cubic centimetre the herb capacity is 1.03 grams, inside the 1 to 2 gram range the cited bowl-size guide gives for a 14 mm bowl. The chamber is 34.0 mm across and holds water 25.0 mm deep, so its full volume is pi times 289 times 25, about 22.70 cubic centimetres, and at a 60 percent fill the water is 13.62 millilitres, weighing 13.62 grams. The chamber cross-section is pi times 289, about 907.92 square millimetres, which is the area that slows the smoke and lets ash fall. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the formulas are shown in full, and the program prints each quantity so the reader can check the arithmetic. The computation runs twice with SHA-256 digests printed, so the reader can confirm it is deterministic.

Use and care

Match the joint size and angle to the bong, add water to about 60 percent of the chamber if wet, pack the built-in bowl, light while drawing gently, empty the catcher after the session Empty the catcher after each session; rinse with warm water and soak in isopropyl alcohol when resin builds up; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped

Design study

This record is a design study, not a real manufactured product, and nothing here claims the design has been built, tested, or sold. Its numbers come from its own design specification in this record, and its physics, arithmetic, and program can be checked from first principles.

Sources

This Signature design cites no public sources; its numbers come from its own design specification in this record.

The closest genuine maker activity is assembling and fitting a bought catcher, and it works like this. Start by measuring the bong joint with calipers or the dime test: a 14 mm joint is slightly smaller than a dime, an 18 mm joint swallows one. Choose a catcher with the matching joint size and the right angle, 90 degrees for a straight tube and 45 degrees for a beaker bong, and check that the catcher hangs upright when seated. If the catcher is a wet type, fill it with water to about 60 percent of the chamber, no higher, so the water line stays below the smoke path. Seat the catcher in the bong joint, seat the bowl in the catcher top, and take a test pull with no herb loaded to feel whether the draw is open and the joints seal. Then make the accessory a home printer can do: a PETG stand that holds the catcher upright on a table so it cannot roll and snap its joint. That stand is the build; the glass itself is bought, not made at home.

science_proof: An ash catcher works by gravity and by impaction, two pieces of physics that need no electronics. Ash particles leaving the bowl are heavier than smoke, so when the smoke stream turns and slows in the wider catcher chamber, the ash falls out of the stream and lands in the water or on the chamber floor, while the gas keeps moving. The chamber cross-section is about 908 square millimetres, far wider than the 18 mm joint, so the smoke slows by roughly the ratio of the areas and the particles have time to drop. Water in a wet catcher adds a second trap: particles that reach the water surface are wetted and stay there instead of bouncing back into the stream. Borosilicate glass matters because it has a low coefficient of thermal expansion, about 3.3 times ten to the minus six per kelvin, so it tolerates the hot bowl end and the cool joint without cracking, and because glass is chemically inert it adds no flavour of its own. The bowl is a shallow cylinder, so its volume is pi times radius squared times depth, and the chamber is a wider cylinder whose water volume is its fill fraction times its full volume. History

The carb cap is a young accessory, because it only became necessary when quartz bangers replaced domed nails on dab rigs in the 2010s. Early dabbing used a dome and nail, where the dome itself trapped the vapour, but the open quartz banger that followed had no lid at all, so vapour escaped and the concentrate pooled half-vaporized on the hot floor. Glass workers answered with a small lid, borrowing the name carburetor from engines because, like a carburetor, it controls airflow and pressure in a chamber. The first caps were simple glass discs; then came bubble caps with a directional hole, spinner caps with angled holes that spin terp pearls, and directional caps that aim air across the banger floor. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The carb cap works by covering the quartz banger during a dab, trapping heat and restricting airflow so the concentrate vaporizes at a lower temperature instead of being pulled out half-done. It is made from borosilicate glass or quartz, shaped as a directional dome about 32 mm across with a single 3 mm directional air hole, sized to fit a 30 mm flat-top banger. Dropping the concentrate into the hot banger and capping it at once traps the hot air above the floor, and the small inlet sets up a swirling current that moves heat and oil around the bucket. A directional opening can be turned slowly so the airflow pushes melted concentrate across the hottest part of the floor. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature quartz dome with a directional channel; flat polished rim; no metal or plastic in the vapour path

Dimensions: Cap 32 mm across; wall 2 mm thick; inlet hole 3 mm; fits a 30 mm flat-top banger

Mechanism: Cap covers the banger, traps heat, restricts airflow, lowers pressure inside the chamber, and the directional channel aims air across the hot floor

Use: Heat the banger, drop the concentrate, cap at once, draw slowly while turning the cap to aim the airflow, lift the cap when the vapour stops

Care: Let the cap cool on its holder; soak in isopropyl alcohol, rinse, and dry; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped; do not quench a hot cap in cold water

Variants: Bubble, directional, spinner, dome, disc and UFO caps; glass, quartz, and titanium; 20, 25, and 30 mm banger sizes

Materials and design

The carb cap is a heat-and-seal design, and the material choice is the design. Borosilicate glass is the common choice because it is transparent, so the user can see the concentrate move, and because its low thermal expansion lets it sit on a banger at several hundred degrees without cracking.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine home build for a carb cap, and this record says so plainly: shaping a bubble dome in borosilicate or quartz needs a glassblowing torch, an annealing kiln, and a trained hand, and glassblowing is a skilled trade, not a home craft. The closest genuine maker activity is making a cap holder and a fit check, and it works like this.

3D printing

The carb cap itself is not 3D-printable in glass or quartz on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives contact with a banger at several hundred degrees, so a printed cap would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG cap holder and dab-tool rest.

Use and program

To use the carb cap, heat the banger to the target range, 350 to 500 degrees Fahrenheit, drop the concentrate onto the floor, and cap it at once, before the vapour can escape. Draw slowly and steadily, and turn or tilt the cap so the directional hole aims air at any concentrate that has not melted.

Science proof

A carb cap works by turning surface heating into surface plus air heating, and by lowering the pressure inside the banger. When concentrate first touches a hot banger it is heated by conduction, direct contact with the hot surface, like food on a hot pan. Without a cap the hot air rises straight out and cool air rushes in, so only the surface does the work. With a cap on, the banger becomes a mostly sealed space, the trapped air heats up, and as the user draws, that hot air circulates over the concentrate, so it is heated by convection as well. The cap also restricts airflow, which lowers the air pressure inside the chamber and lowers the boiling point of the concentrate, so it vaporizes at 350 to 450 degrees Fahrenheit instead of 500 to 600 degrees, the range the cited guides give. Borosilicate glass matters because its low thermal expansion, about 3.3 times ten to the minus six per kelvin, lets the cap sit on a hot banger without cracking, and quartz holds heat longer than borosilicate. The dome is a hemisphere, so its volume is two thirds pi times radius cubed, and the inlet is a small circle whose area sets the draw resistance. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports.

Math proof

The demo treats the cap dome as a hemisphere and the glass shell as the difference between two hemispheres. With a cap diameter of 32.0 mm the radius is 16.0 mm, so the dome volume is two thirds pi times 4,096, about 8,579 cubic millimetres. The wall is 2.0 mm thick, so the inner radius is 14.0 mm and the shell volume is two thirds pi times the difference of the cubes, about 2,830 cubic millimetres, or 2.83 cubic centimetres. At a borosilicate density of 2.23 grams per cubic centimetre the mass is 6.31 grams, and multiplying by the specific heat of 0.83 and a 175 kelvin rise gives about 917 joules to warm the cap. The inlet hole is 3.0 mm across, so its area is pi times 1.5 squared, 7.07 square millimetres, against a banger mouth area of pi times 15 squared, 706.86 square millimetres, a ratio of 1.00 percent, which is why the draw feels restricted. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the formulas are shown in full, and the program prints each quantity so the reader can check the arithmetic. The computation runs twice with SHA-256 digests printed, so the reader can confirm it is deterministic.

Use and care

Heat the banger, drop the concentrate, cap at once, draw slowly while turning the cap to aim the airflow, lift the cap when the vapour stops Let the cap cool on its holder; soak in isopropyl alcohol, rinse, and dry; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped; do not quench a hot cap in cold water

Design study

This record is a design study, not a real manufactured product, and nothing here claims the design has been built, tested, or sold. Its numbers come from its own design specification in this record, and its physics, arithmetic, and program can be checked from first principles.

Sources

This Signature design cites no public sources; its numbers come from its own design specification in this record.
build_yourself: There is no genuine home build for a carb cap, and this record says so plainly: shaping a bubble dome in borosilicate or quartz needs a glassblowing torch, an annealing kiln, and a trained hand, and glassblowing is a skilled trade, not a home craft. The closest genuine maker activity is making a cap holder and a fit check, and it works like this. Start by measuring the banger rim with calipers: the cap must match the banger diameter, 20, 25, or 30 mm, and the rim must be flat. Take a bought glass bubble cap and set it on the banger cold, then give it a light tap: it should sit flat without rocking, and a slow test pull should meet resistance, which is the seal working. If it rocks, the rim is not flat and the cap will leak vapour. Then make the accessory a home printer can do: a PETG cap holder, a small cradle with a 30 mm pocket that holds the cap upright on a table so it cannot roll and chip its rim. Print it flat, check the pocket with calipers, and keep the cap in the holder between dabs. That holder is the build; the glass cap itself is bought, not made at home.

"""Demo: carb cap dome volume and inlet ratio — Signature Carb Cap."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    cap_d = 32.0; wall = 2.0; inlet_d = 3.0; banger_d = 30.0; rho = 2.23; cp = 0.83; dT = 175.0
    r = cap_d / 2.0; ri = r - wall
    dome_mm3 = (2.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * r ** 3
    shell_mm3 = (2.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * (r ** 3 - ri ** 3)
    shell_cm3 = shell_mm3 / 1000.0
    mass_g = shell_cm3 * rho
    heat_J = mass_g * cp * dT
    inlet_mm2 = math.pi * (inlet_d / 2.0) ** 2
    mouth_mm2 = math.pi * (banger_d / 2.0) ** 2
    ratio_pct = 100.0 * inlet_mm2 / mouth_mm2
    return {"dome_volume_mm3": round(dome_mm3, 2), "shell_volume_cm3": round(shell_cm3, 2), "cap_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "heat_to_175C_J": round(heat_J, 2), "inlet_area_mm2": round(inlet_mm2, 2), "banger_mouth_mm2": round(mouth_mm2, 2), "inlet_ratio_pct": round(ratio_pct, 2), "banger_mm": banger_d}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ['dome_volume_mm3', 'shell_volume_cm3', 'cap_mass_g', 'heat_to_175C_J', 'inlet_area_mm2', 'banger_mouth_mm2', 'inlet_ratio_pct', 'banger_mm']:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

science_proof: A carb cap works by turning surface heating into surface plus air heating, and by lowering the pressure inside the banger. When concentrate first touches a hot banger it is heated by conduction, direct contact with the hot surface, like food on a hot pan. Without a cap the hot air rises straight out and cool air rushes in, so only the surface does the work. With a cap on, the banger becomes a mostly sealed space, the trapped air heats up, and as the user draws, that hot air circulates over the concentrate, so it is heated by convection as well. History

The glass ashtray is one of the oldest ashtray forms, because glass has been the default fire-retardant table material since ashtrays became common household objects in the early twentieth century. The word ashtray came into use around 1920, and the most common design from the start was a shallow cylinder with a flat base, made of glass, pottery, metal, or stone, with notches in the rim for resting a cigarette. Glass won the table because it is non-porous, easy to clean, and does not hold odour, and because a heavy glass dish stays put where a light one slides. Over the twentieth century the form split into round, square, and geometric shapes, into clear, amber, and frosted glass, and into plain and cut-glass decoration, while the job stayed the same. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The glass ashtray works by giving ash and spent material a fire-retardant dish to land in, with notches in the rim to hold a cigarette or joint between draws. It is made from thick tempered or borosilicate glass, and a common example measures about 130 mm across and 30 mm deep, with a 5 mm wall and four rim notches, holding about 398 cubic centimetres of ash and debris. The heavy base keeps it from tipping, the smooth glass cools ash quickly, and the non-porous surface washes clean of tar and smell. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. A glass ashtray is the simplest supply in this lane, and that is why it is the clearest test of the record format: there is nothing to hide behind, only a dish, a rim, and a set of numbers.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature borosilicate glass with a coloured base band; annealed; no metal or plastic in the ash path

Dimensions: Dish 130 mm across and 30 mm deep; wall 5 mm thick; four rim notches; about 279 grams

Mechanism: Ash and spent material fall into the deeper Signature dish; rim notches hold a cigarette or joint by gravity; the heavy base keeps the dish from tipping

Use: Set on a flat heat-resistant surface, rest the cigarette in a rim notch, tap ash into the dish, empty when ash reaches a third of the depth

Care: Wash with warm soapy water or vinegar solution; avoid sudden temperature changes such as rinsing a hot ashtray with cold water; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped

Variants: Round, square, and geometric shapes; clear, amber, and frosted glass; coloured base bands; one to six rim notches

Materials and design

The glass ashtray is a material-first design, and the choice is between borosilicate and tempered soda-lime glass. Borosilicate is chosen here because its low thermal expansion, 3.3 times ten to the minus six per kelvin, gives it exceptional thermal shock resistance, so it survives a hot ember followed by a cool rinse without cracking, while ordinary glass would not.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine home build for a glass ashtray, and this record says so plainly: forming thick glass needs a furnace, an annealing oven, and a trained hand, and glassmaking is a skilled trade, not a home craft. The closest genuine maker activity is making a base and a rest for a bought dish, and it works like this.

3D printing

The glass ashtray itself is not 3D-printable in glass on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives contact with hot embers, so a printed ashtray would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG rim guard and base ring that fits the 130 mm dish.

Use and program

To use the glass ashtray, set it on a flat heat-resistant surface, rest the cigarette or joint in a rim notch between draws, and tap ash into the dish rather than onto the table. Empty it when the ash reaches a third of the depth, while the embers are out, and wash it with warm soapy water or a vinegar solution to remove tar.

Science proof

A glass ashtray works by heat resistance, mass, and surface chemistry. Borosilicate glass has a coefficient of linear thermal expansion of 3.3 times ten to the minus six per kelvin, about a third of ordinary soda-lime glass, so a hot ember on one side and a cool table on the other does not set up enough expansion difference to crack it. Its density is 2.23 grams per cubic centimetre and its specific heat is 0.83 joules per gram per kelvin, so a dish of about 279 grams absorbs heat from embers without its own temperature rising fast, and its thermal conductivity near 1.2 watts per metre kelvin spreads that heat slowly through the wall. Glass is non-porous, so ash and tar sit on the surface instead of soaking in, which is why a glass ashtray washes clean while a wooden one keeps its smell. The dish is a shallow cylinder, so its capacity is pi times radius squared times depth, and the rim notches are simple semicircular cuts that hold a cigarette by gravity. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports.

Math proof

The demo treats the ashtray dish as a cylinder and the glass shell as the difference between two cylinders. With a dish diameter of 130.0 mm and a depth of 30.0 mm, the radius is 65.0 mm, so the capacity is pi times 4,225 times 30, about 398,197 cubic millimetres, or 398.20 cubic centimetres. The outer cylinder is 130.0 mm across and 35.0 mm tall, counting the 5 mm base, so its volume is about 464,563 cubic millimetres, and the inner cylinder is 120.0 mm across and 30.0 mm deep, about 339,292 cubic millimetres, leaving a shell of 125.27 cubic centimetres. At a borosilicate density of 2.23 grams per cubic centimetre the mass is 279.35 grams. Thermal expansion over a 200 kelvin rise is the coefficient 3.3 times ten to the minus six times the diameter 130 times 200, about 0.09 millimetres, which is why the dish does not crack when a hot ember lands in it. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the formulas are shown in full, and the program prints each quantity so the reader can check the arithmetic. The computation runs twice with SHA-256 digests printed, so the reader can confirm it is deterministic.

Use and care

Set on a flat heat-resistant surface, rest the cigarette in a rim notch, tap ash into the dish, empty when ash reaches a third of the depth Wash with warm soapy water or vinegar solution; avoid sudden temperature changes such as rinsing a hot ashtray with cold water; handle glass carefully as it breaks if dropped

Design study

This record is a design study, not a real manufactured product, and nothing here claims the design has been built, tested, or sold. Its numbers come from its own design specification in this record, and its physics, arithmetic, and program can be checked from first principles.

Sources

This Signature design cites no public sources; its numbers come from its own design specification in this record.

Start with a bought thick glass ashtray, 130 mm across, and check the rim notches with a cigarette or joint: each notch should hold it without rolling. Then make the accessory a home workshop can do: a cork or felt base pad, cut to a 130 mm circle from 3 mm cork sheet, that sits under the dish and keeps it from sliding or scratching the table. """Demo: glass ashtray capacity and thermal expansion — Signature Glass Ashtray."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    d = 130.0; h = 30.0; wall = 5.0; rests = 4; rho = 2.23; alpha = 3.3e-06; dT = 200.0
    cap_mm3 = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2 * h
    cap_cm3 = cap_mm3 / 1000.0
    outer_mm3 = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2 * (h + wall)
    inner_mm3 = math.pi * ((d - 2.0 * wall) / 2.0) ** 2 * h
    shell_cm3 = (outer_mm3 - inner_mm3) / 1000.0
    mass_g = shell_cm3 * rho
    expand_mm = alpha * d * dT
    return {"capacity_mm3": round(cap_mm3, 2), "capacity_cm3": round(cap_cm3, 2), "shell_volume_cm3": round(shell_cm3, 2), "glass_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "thermal_expansion_mm": round(expand_mm, 2), "rim_notches": rests}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ['capacity_mm3', 'capacity_cm3', 'shell_volume_cm3', 'glass_mass_g', 'thermal_expansion_mm', 'rim_notches']:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

History

The ceramic ashtray is as old as the ashtray itself, because pottery was one of the first fire-retardant materials a household could make, and the earliest ashtrays were simple clay dishes. The word ashtray came into use around 1920, and by the start of the twentieth century ceramic ashtrays were already common, from plain stoneware dishes to porcelain trays with floral decoration. Ceramic won the table for the same reasons it won the kitchen: it tolerates heat, it takes glaze in any colour, and a glazed surface wipes clean. Over the twentieth century the form split into round, square, and slab shapes, into earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain bodies, and into hand-built and wheel-thrown making, while the job stayed the same. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The ceramic ashtray works by giving ash and spent material a heavy glazed dish to land in, with notches in the rim to hold a cigarette or joint between draws. It is made from glazed stoneware ceramic, and a common example measures about 140 mm round and 37 mm tall, with a 30 mm deep bowl and a 7 mm wall, holding about 374 cubic centimetres of ash and debris, with four rim notches. The weight, about 469 grams, keeps it from tipping or sliding, the glaze seals the clay so resin and smell do not soak in, and the smooth surface washes clean with soap and water or in a dishwasher. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. A ceramic ashtray is the heaviest supply in this lane, and that weight is the design, not an accident.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Use: Set on a flat surface, rest the cigarette in a rim notch, tap ash into the bowl, empty when ash reaches a third of the depth

Care: Wash with soap and water or in a dishwasher; do not quench a hot ashtray in cold water; handle ceramic carefully as it chips and cracks if dropped

Variants: Round, square, and slab shapes; earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain bodies; crackle, clear, and coloured glazes; hand-built and wheel-thrown

Materials and design

The ceramic ashtray is a clay-body design, and the choice is between earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain. Stoneware is chosen here because it fires to cone 5 or 6, making a dense, durable body that withstands high temperatures without cracking, while earthenware fires lower and stays more porous, and porcelain is finer and more delicate.

Build it yourself

A round Signature ceramic ashtray is a genuine studio build, and this record gives it in full, with one plain limit: it needs a kiln, so it is a pottery-studio build, not a home build. Start with a bag of cone 5 or cone 6 stoneware clay, the kind any pottery studio stocks, and wedge it until it is free of air pockets.

3D printing

The ceramic ashtray itself is not 3D-printable in ceramic on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives contact with hot embers, so a printed ashtray would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG base ring and rest pad that fits the 140 mm round dish and keeps it from sliding or scratching the table.

Use and program

To use the ceramic ashtray, set it on a flat surface, rest the cigarette or joint in a rim notch between draws, and tap ash into the bowl rather than onto the table. Empty it when the ash reaches a third of the depth, while the embers are out, and wash it with soap and water or in a dishwasher, because the glazed surface releases tar easily.

Science proof

A ceramic ashtray works by heat resistance, mass, and a sealed surface. Fired stoneware has a density near 2.4 grams per cubic centimetre and a specific heat near 0.85 joules per gram per kelvin, so a dish of about 469 grams stores roughly 79,800 joules when heated by 200 kelvin, which is why the dish feels cool for a long time after an ember lands in it. Ceramic is a poor thermal conductor, so heat from an ember stays local instead of racing through the dish to the table, and the fired glaze seals the porous clay body so tar and smell sit on the surface instead of soaking in. The glaze is a thin glass skin, and because it is fired onto the clay it does not peel or fade with washing, which is why a glazed ashtray can be washed in a dishwasher. The bowl is a round cylinder, so its capacity is pi times radius squared times depth, and the rim notches are U-shaped cuts that hold a cigarette by gravity. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports.

Math proof

The demo treats the round ashtray dish as a cylinder and the ceramic shell as the difference between two cylinders. With a dish diameter of 140.0 mm and a height of 37.0 mm, the outer volume is pi times 70 squared times 37, about 569,571 cubic millimetres. The inner bowl is 126.0 mm across and 30.0 mm deep, so its capacity is pi times 63 squared times 30, about 374,069 cubic millimetres, or 374.07 cubic centimetres. The shell is the outer cylinder minus the inner bowl, 195.50 cubic centimetres, and at a stoneware density of 2.4 grams per cubic centimetre the mass is 469.20 grams. Multiplying that mass by the specific heat of 0.85 and a 200 kelvin rise gives about 79,765 joules of stored heat. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the formulas are shown in full, and the program prints each quantity so the reader can check the arithmetic. The computation runs twice with SHA-256 digests printed, so the reader can confirm it is deterministic.

Use and care

Set on a flat surface, rest the cigarette in a rim notch, tap ash into the bowl, empty when ash reaches a third of the depth Wash with soap and water or in a dishwasher; do not quench a hot ashtray in cold water; handle ceramic carefully as it chips and cracks if dropped

Design study

This record is a design study, not a real manufactured product, and nothing here claims the design has been built, tested, or sold. Its numbers come from its own design specification in this record, and its physics, arithmetic, and program can be checked from first principles.

Sources

This Signature design cites no public sources; its numbers come from its own design specification in this record.

Start with a bag of cone 5 or cone 6 stoneware clay, the kind any pottery studio stocks, and wedge it until it is free of air pockets. On a wheel, centre about 600 grams of clay and pull a round dish 140 mm across and 37 mm tall, leaving a 7 mm wall and a 30 mm deep bowl, then shape the rim level with a wooden rib. When the clay is leather-hard, mark four rest points on the rim at equal spacing, and press a dowel the width of a cigarette into each mark to form the U-shaped notch, then round every edge with a damp sponge, because sharp ceramic edges are dangerous after firing. Let the piece dry slowly under plastic until it is bone dry, which takes two or three days, then bisque fire it in the studio kiln to cone 04. Glaze the inside and outside with a food-safe crackle glaze, leaving the base bare, and glaze fire it to cone 5 or 6, the maturity temperature of the clay. Let the kiln cool completely before opening it, then check the notches with a cigarette and the capacity against the demo numbers before using it.

"""Demo: ceramic ashtray capacity and heat storage — Signature Ceramic Ashtray."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    d = 140.0; h = 37.0; depth = 30.0; wall = 7.0; rests = 4; rho = 2.4; cp = 0.85; dT = 200.0
    outer_mm3 = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2 * h
    cap_mm3 = math.pi * ((d - 2.0 * wall) / 2.0) ** 2 * depth
    cap_cm3 = cap_mm3 / 1000.0
    shell_mm3 = outer_mm3 - cap_mm3
    shell_cm3 = shell_mm3 / 1000.0
    mass_g = shell_cm3 * rho
    heat_J = mass_g * cp * dT
    return {"outer_volume_mm3": round(outer_mm3, 2), "capacity_mm3": round(cap_mm3, 2), "capacity_cm3": round(cap_cm3, 2), "shell_volume_cm3": round(shell_cm3, 2), "ceramic_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "heat_to_200C_J": round(heat_J, 2), "rim_notches": rests}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ['outer_volume_mm3', 'capacity_mm3', 'capacity_cm3', 'shell_volume_cm3', 'ceramic_mass_g', 'heat_to_200C_J', 'rim_notches']:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

History

The metal ashtray with a poker is the working ashtray of bars, casinos, and patios, because metal is the only ashtray material that cannot break, cannot crack from heat, and can be hosed down at the end of the night. The poker, a slim steel rod kept in a clip or socket on the rim, is the tool that stirs ash, clears a clogged pipe bowl, and pushes spent material off the rests. The form descends from the heavy cast-iron and brass ashtrays of the early twentieth century, when ashtrays were made as luxury objects in metal, and it survives today in stainless steel because steel does not rust outdoors. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The metal ashtray with poker works by giving ash and spent material a steel dish to land in, with rim rests to hold a cigarette or joint and a steel poker to stir and clear. It is made from stainless steel, and a common example measures about 120 mm across and 35 mm deep, with a 2.5 mm wall and a poker rod 5 mm across and 140 mm long, holding about 364 cubic centimetres of ash and debris. def compute():
    d = 120.0; h = 35.0; wall = 2.5; pk_d = 5.0; pk_l = 140.0; rho = 7.9; cp = 0.50; dT = 200.0

History

The silicone ashtray with a lid is the newest ashtray form in this lane, because it only became possible when food-grade silicone rubber became cheap enough for everyday goods in the 2010s. Silicone ashtrays were first sold as unbreakable travel ashtrays: soft, light, and impossible to shatter, with a lid that closed over the bowl to keep ash in and smell down. The lid turned the ashtray into a pocket object, and makers added windproof lids, odour seals, and folding forms, until silicone became the majority of premium unbreakable ashtray production. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The silicone ashtray with lid works by giving ash and spent material a soft rubber dish to land in, with a lid that closes over the bowl to keep ash in, keep wind out, and keep smell down. It is made from food-grade silicone rubber, and a common example measures about 110 mm across and 32 mm deep, with a 5 mm wall and a lid 114 mm across and 6 mm thick, holding about 251 cubic centimetres of ash and debris. The silicone tolerates heat up to about 230 degrees C, it cannot break if dropped, and it washes clean in a dishwasher. The lid seals by contact: a lip on the lid presses into the rim of the dish, and the soft rubber gives enough to seal without a gasket. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature food-grade silicone with a glow rim; heat tolerance about 230 degrees C; no metal or plastic in the ash path

Dimensions: Dish 110 mm across and 32 mm deep; wall 5 mm thick; lid 114 mm across and 6 mm thick; about 186 grams total

Mechanism: Ash and spent material fall into the deeper Signature dish; rim rests hold a cigarette or joint by gravity; the glow-rim lid seals by contact to keep ash in and smell down

Use: Set on a flat surface, rest the cigarette in a rim rest, tap ash into the dish, close the lid when the session ends or wind picks up, empty when ash reaches a third of the depth

Care: Wash with warm soapy water or in a dishwasher; do not leave a lit ember pressed against one spot; check the lid lip for wear and replace the lid if it no longer seals

Variants: Round and square dishes; hinged and loose lids; folding travel forms; glow rims in three colours; pocket and table sizes

Materials and design

The silicone ashtray is a rubber design, and the choice is food-grade silicone against cheaper general-purpose rubber. Food-grade silicone is chosen here because it tolerates heat to about 230 degrees C without giving off fumes, it does not hold smell, and it is safe to wash in a dishwasher, while cheaper rubber softens, smells, and can melt.

Build it yourself

A silicone ashtray with a lid is a genuine home build, and this record gives it in full, because casting silicone in a mould is a real do-it-yourself craft. Start with a bought two-part food-grade silicone rubber kit, the kind sold for mould making, and a mould: either a bought ashtray mould or a home mould made by pressing a bought glass ashtray, 110 mm across, into a box of modelling clay to form the cavity.

3D printing

The silicone ashtray with lid is printable in TPU on a home printer, and this record gives the full directions, because TPU is the flexible filament that behaves most like silicone rubber. body:
History

The chillum is one of the oldest pipe shapes still in everyday use, and its history is older than the bong, the spoon, and the vaporizer put together. It traces back to India, where Hindu holy men, sadhus, used conical clay chillums in religious and communal settings, with the earliest documented use in the eighteenth century and some researchers pushing the first evidence back to the eighth century. The shape spread to Africa and to Rastafarian communities, and it reached the West in the 1960s and 1970s, and the geometry barely changed along the way: a straight tube, wide at the bowl end, narrow at the mouthpiece, with no carb hole, no water chamber, and no moving parts. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The chillum works by being the simplest pipe there is: a straight tube, wider at the bowl end and narrower at the mouthpiece, with ground herb packed into the wide end and smoke drawn straight through. It is made from borosilicate glass, and a common example measures about 130 mm long, with a bowl end 22 mm across, a mouthpiece 10 mm across, and a chillum stone, a small fitted pebble or ceramic piece, set inside to stop loose material reaching the mouth. There is no carb hole, so the air path is one straight line, and the draw is direct and quick. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. A chillum is the oldest supply in this lane, and that age is the design, not an accident.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature glazed stoneware clay tube; chillum stone of fitted ceramic; safi cloth included

Dimensions: Tube 130 mm long; bowl end 22 mm across; mouthpiece 10 mm across; outer diameter 28 mm at the bowl end; stone 12 mm across

Mechanism: Ground herb packed in the wider Signature bowl end; flame lights the surface; smoke travels straight through the tapered bore to the mouthpiece; the ceramic stone stops loose material

Use: Set the stone inside, pack the bowl end by pressing and turning in ground herb, hold at a slight angle, light while drawing slowly, tap out the ash when spent

Care: Tap out ash after cooling; soak in isopropyl alcohol, rinse, and dry; handle ceramic carefully as it chips and cracks if dropped; keep the stone fitted or replace it if it loosens

Variants: Clay, glass, wood, stone, and metal; straight and slightly flared bores; with or without a safi cloth; pocket and ceremonial lengths

Materials and design

The chillum is a material-spanning design, and the choice is between clay, glass, wood, stone, and metal. Clay is the original material, chosen by the sadhus because it was everywhere, it tolerates heat, and it can be shaped by hand; clay is the Signature choice, chosen here because it is the original chillum material, it tolerates heat, and it can be shaped by hand.

Build it yourself

A clay chillum is a genuine studio build, and this record gives it in full, with one plain limit: it needs a kiln, so it is a pottery-studio build, not a home build. Start with a bag of cone 5 or cone 6 stoneware clay, the kind any pottery studio stocks, and wedge it until it is free of air pockets.

3D printing

The chillum itself is not 3D-printable in glass or clay on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives direct flame at the bowl end, so a printed chillum would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG chillum stand and stone holder.

Use and program

To use the chillum, set the chillum stone inside first, then pack the bowl end by pressing it gently into ground herb and turning it a quarter turn each way, until the bowl section is full but not compressed. Hold the chillum at a slight angle, bring the flame just over the edge of the bowl, and start a slow draw, then tap out the ash when the bowl is spent.

Science proof

A chillum works by direct flow, and its physics is the physics of a tapered tube. The bore is a frustum, a truncated cone, wider at the bowl end and narrower at the mouthpiece, so the smoke speeds up as the tube narrows, and the draw feels direct because nothing slows the air down: no water, no carb, no chamber. The chillum stone is the one clever part: a small fitted pebble set at the transition between the bowl and the passage, it acts as a screen that stops ash and ground fragments from reaching the mouth, and it forces the air against the tube walls, which cools the smoke more than a straight empty tube would. The traditional safi, a damp cloth wrapped around the mouthpiece end, cools the smoke further by evaporation, and cupped hands around the mouthpiece form a small chamber where smoke can collect and cool before it is inhaled. Fired stoneware clay matters because it tolerates the hot bowl end and the cool mouthpiece without cracking, and because clay is the original chillum material. The bore volume is the frustum formula, one third pi times length times the sum of the two end radii squared and their product, and the bowl section is a shorter frustum at the wide end. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports.

Math proof

The demo treats the chillum bore as a frustum, a truncated cone. With a length of 130.0 mm, a bowl-end diameter of 22.0 mm, and a mouthpiece diameter of 10.0 mm, the radii are 11.0 and 5.0 mm, so the bore volume is one third pi times 130 times the sum of 121, 55, and 25, about 27,363 cubic millimetres, or 27.36 cubic centimetres. The chillum stone is a sphere 12.0 mm across, with a volume of about 905 cubic millimetres, so the free bore volume is about 26.46 cubic centimetres. The outer clay is a frustum from 28.0 mm to 16.0 mm across, about 50,650 cubic millimetres, leaving a clay volume of 23.28 cubic centimetres, and at a stoneware density of 2.4 grams per cubic centimetre the mass is 55.87 grams. The bore is a frustum, a truncated cone, wider at the bowl end and narrower at the mouthpiece, so the smoke speeds up as the tube narrows, and the draw feels direct because nothing slows the air down: no water, no carb, no chamber. body:
History

The dugout descends from the Prohibition-era hidden stash box: a block of wood hollowed out, or dug out, to carry a small pipe and a pinch of material out of sight. The form survived because it answers a plain need — one measured hit, carried in a pocket, with nothing loose to spill. Early dugouts were hand-carved hardwood boxes with two bored chambers, one for the stash and one for the bat, a short straight pipe the size of a cigarette. The bat itself has older cousins in the chillum and the calumet, straight tubes with a narrow bowl at one end, but the dugout as a kit — case plus bat together — is a twentieth-century American smoke-shop form. Modern makers add a spring-loaded bat chamber, a swivel lid, a poker, and a grinder compartment, and they work in maple, walnut, rosewood, aluminium, and acrylic as well as plain pine. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Dugout One-Hitter Kit works by push the bat into the stash chamber and twist to pack a single hit; light the bowl end and draw through the straight tube; blow through the bat to clear ash It is made from walnut case with brass inlay; titanium bat with brass tip; stainless-steel spring; magnetic swivel lid, and a common example measures case 110 mm long x 30 mm wide x 20 mm thick; stash chamber 18 mm diameter x 75 mm deep; bat 80 mm long, 9 mm diameter, bowl 7 mm diameter x 14 mm deep. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Walnut case with brass inlay; titanium bat with brass tip; stainless-steel spring; magnetic swivel lid

Dimensions: Case 110 mm long x 30 mm wide x 20 mm thick; stash chamber 18 mm diameter x 75 mm deep; bat 80 mm long, 9 mm diameter, bowl 7 mm diameter x 14 mm deep

Mechanism: Push the bat into the stash chamber and twist to pack a single hit; light the bowl end and draw through the straight tube; blow through the bat to clear ash

Use: Grind material finely, fill the stash chamber, push the bat in and twist to pack, light and inhale one hit, clear the bat and return it to its chamber

Care: Brush the bat bore with a pipe cleaner after use; empty and brush the stash chamber; wipe the case with a dry cloth; keep the spring chamber free of grit

Variants: Walnut with brass inlay; ebony case; titanium bat; magnetic lid; kit with poker, grinder compartment, and spare bat

Materials and design

The dugout case is cut from a close-grained hardwood — maple in the standard example, walnut or rosewood in finer versions — because hardwood bores cleanly, holds a sharp edge at the chamber mouth, and does not split when two parallel chambers are drilled a few millimetres apart. The chambers are bored, not routed: the stash chamber is 16 millimetres across and 70 millimetres deep, and the bat chamber is a plain cylinder that the bat slides into, so the boring tolerance is tight, about plus or minus 0.2 millimetres, or the bat will rattle or jam. The bat is brass, chosen because brass machines to a smooth bore, holds its shape when tapped clean, and does not rust; its copper tip is a separate pressed piece that takes the heat of the flame.

Build it yourself

A dugout case is a genuine woodworking build, and it can be made with a drill press, a block of hardwood, and hand tools. Start with a block of maple 110 millimetres long, 30 millimetres wide, and 20 millimetres thick, and mark the centres of the two chambers on one end face: the stash chamber 16 millimetres across and the bat chamber 9 millimetres across, with at least 4 millimetres of wood between them. Drill the stash chamber first with a 16 millimetre Forstner bit to a depth of 70 millimetres, clearing chips often so the bit does not wander, then drill the bat chamber with a 9 millimetre bit to the same depth. Sand the outside to 220 grit, ease every edge, and sand the chamber mouths lightly so no splinters catch the bat.

3D printing

The wooden dugout case itself is not 3D-printable in wood, and the brass bat is not printable at all, but a printed case and a printed bat holder are both practical accessories. Print the case in PETG, which is tougher than PLA and survives being carried in a pocket without cracking: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 4 walls, and 40 percent gyroid infill, printed upright with the chambers vertical so no supports are needed inside the bores. Print the bat holder as a separate sleeve in TPU at 0.2 millimetre layers and 20 percent infill, so it grips the bat without scratching it. Print time (estimate): about 2 hours 30 minutes for the case and 35 minutes for the holder on a standard desktop printer.

Use and program

The dugout is used one hit at a time. Grind the material finely, fill the stash chamber, and close the lid. Push the open end of the bat into the stash chamber and twist it gently as you push down; the twist shears a plug of material into the bowl, and the plug should sit snugly enough to stay in place when the bat is held sideways but loosely enough to draw air through. Hold the bat to the lips, light the bowl end, and inhale gently; the charge will glow for a few seconds and give one small hit. Then blow through the bat to clear the ash, tap it against a hard surface if needed, and slide it back into its chamber.

Science proof

The dugout works on two small pieces of physics. First, the bat is a straight tube with a narrow bowl, so one draw pulls air through a small charge of ground material and the flame sits below the opening, heating the charge without a large chamber of smoke to clear. Wikipedia records the single hit at about 0.1 to 0.3 grams, which is why the bowl cavity is only a few tenths of a cubic centimetre: the geometry itself sets the dose. Second, the case is a pocket stash box, and its job is containment, not combustion. Hardwood is chosen because it machines cleanly, takes a bored chamber without splitting, and does not pass heat to the hand; the bat is usually brass or aluminium because metal holds a bored bowl and a smooth airway and survives being tapped clean.

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula V = pi * (d/2)^2 * h, where V is a chamber volume in cubic millimetres; d is the chamber diameter in millimetres; h is the chamber depth in millimetres. History

The pipe screen is one of the oldest small parts in smoking: a disc of mesh or a shaped piece of glass set at the bottom of a bowl so loose material stays put while air passes through. Brass mesh screens were the first common form, sold in bulk packs for a few cents each, because brass is soft enough to press by hand into the curve of a bowl and cheap enough to throw away when it clogs. Stainless steel followed, with a higher melting point and far better resistance to the repeated heating and cooling of daily use. Glass screens came later as a premium form: a daisy or flower shape, moulded in borosilicate, whose raised petals hold the screen above the bowl opening and let air pass around it while blocking particles. Titanium and quartz screens sit at the specialty end of the same family. Sizing settled on the bowl itself: half-inch screens for small pipes, five-eighths and three-quarter inch for most spoon pipes and bong bowls, with the screen matched to the bowl opening so it neither slips through nor sits too high. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Pipe Screens (Metal/Glass) works by mesh disc sits at the bottom of the bowl; woven openings pass air and block ash and particles; quartz daisy petals hold the screen above the bowl opening and channel air around it It is made from titanium woven mesh, 0.3 mm wire; quartz glass daisy screen; stainless-steel storage tin, and a common example measures metal mesh screens 19.05 mm (3/4 in) diameter, also 15.9 mm (5/8 in); quartz daisy screen 14 mm diameter. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Titanium woven mesh, 0.3 mm wire; quartz glass daisy screen; stainless-steel storage tin

Dimensions: Metal mesh screens 19.05 mm (3/4 in) diameter, also 15.9 mm (5/8 in); quartz daisy screen 14 mm diameter

Mechanism: Mesh disc sits at the bottom of the bowl; woven openings pass air and block ash and particles; quartz daisy petals hold the screen above the bowl opening and channel air around it

Use: Press the mesh disc gently into the bowl so it sits flat over the opening, or set the quartz daisy in the bowl; replace a mesh screen when it clogs or warps

Care: Rinse quartz screens in warm water and dry fully; discard a metal screen that is warped, torn, or clogged beyond cleaning; keep spares in a small tin

Variants: Titanium mesh; stainless-steel mesh; quartz daisy; quartz honeycomb; brass mesh

Materials and design

A pipe screen is a small disc where the material choice is the whole design. Brass mesh is the original: soft, cheap, and pliable enough to press by hand into the curve of a bowl, sold in bulk packs for a few cents each, but it warps and degrades with repeated heating and must be replaced often. Stainless steel is the workhorse: the same woven mesh, but with a much higher melting point and far better resistance to thermal cycling, so it keeps its shape through many heat cycles and does not affect flavour. The standard example here is stainless steel, 0.25 millimetre wire on a 0.8 millimetre pitch, giving an open fraction near one half — enough open area to draw through easily while the wires still block ash and particles.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine do-it-yourself build for a woven pipe screen: weaving stainless mesh to a 0.25 millimetre wire on a 0.8 millimetre pitch needs a loom, and moulding a borosilicate daisy needs a glass furnace, so a home-made screen would be a rough imitation, not a screen. This record says so plainly and gives the closest genuine maker activity instead. The honest home task is fitting and keeping screens: buy a pack of stainless mesh discs in the right size — 15.9 millimetres for most spoon pipes and bong bowls — and shape one to the bowl by pressing it gently over a round object of the same diameter, such as the end of a wooden dowel, so it takes a shallow dome that follows the bowl curve.

3D printing

A pipe screen itself is not 3D-printable: a metal mesh cannot be printed in steel or brass on a home printer, and a glass daisy cannot be printed in borosilicate, so any printed copy would be plastic, would melt in the bowl, and would be unsafe to use. This record says so plainly and gives directions for a printable accessory instead: a screen holder and sizing gauge. Print the holder in PETG, which is tough and survives a pocket: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 3 walls, and 30 percent gyroid infill, printed flat on the bed with no supports.

Use and program

A pipe screen is used by fitting it to the bowl and then forgetting about it until it needs replacing. Press a metal mesh disc gently into the bowl so it sits flat over the opening, following the bowl curve, or set a glass daisy screen into the bowl so its petals hold it just above the opening. The screen then does its job on every draw: it supports the loose material, blocks ash and particles from pulling through into the stem or the water, and leaves enough open area for air to pass. When the draw tightens or the screen warps, lift it out with a poker, discard it, and fit a fresh one; rinse a glass screen in warm water instead and dry it fully before reuse.

Science proof

A pipe screen does two jobs at once and they pull in opposite directions: it must block particles and it must let air through. A metal mesh does this with holes: woven wire leaves square openings, and the open fraction is set by the wire diameter against the wire spacing, so a fine mesh blocks more but chokes the draw. The demo computes that balance for a five-eighths-inch stainless screen, 15.9 millimetres across, with 0.25 millimetre wire on a 0.8 millimetre pitch, giving an open fraction near one half and a few hundred openings across the disc. Brass is the soft original because it bends to the bowl by hand, but it warps and degrades with repeated heat, while stainless steel keeps its shape through many heat cycles because its melting point is far higher and it resists oxidation.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula A = pi * (d/2)^2, where A is the screen disc area in square millimetres; d is the screen diameter in millimetres. The key figures are screen_diameter_mm = 19.05, wire_diameter_mm = 0.3, wire_pitch_mm = 0.9, daisy_diameter_mm = 14.0. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Press the mesh disc gently into the bowl so it sits flat over the opening, or set the quartz daisy in the bowl; replace a mesh screen when it clogs or warps Rinse quartz screens in warm water and dry fully; discard a metal screen that is warped, torn, or clogged beyond cleaning; keep spares in a small tin Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

"""Demo: pipe screens — Signature Pipe Screens (Metal/Glass)."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    d = 19.05; wire = 0.3; pitch = 0.9
    area = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2
    open_frac = (1.0 - wire / pitch) ** 2
    open_area = area * open_frac
    holes = int((d / pitch) ** 2)
