History

The mini bong is a full-size water pipe reduced to pocket scale: the same beaker or straight tube, the same downstem and bowl, the same water filtration, in a piece under about eight inches tall. Small water pipes are not new — bubblers and pocket pipes have been sold for decades — but the mini bong as a named type grew with borosilicate glassmaking, which made a thin, heat-resistant tube cheap enough to shrink without cracking. The sources put most mini bongs between four and seven inches tall: four to five inches for the most portable pieces, six to seven inches for a longer smoke path and a larger chamber that is easier to clear. The beaker base became the common form because its wide foot holds more water and keeps a small piece planted on a table, while the straight tube stays the most compact. A six-inch beaker with a 10 or 14 millimetre joint, a removable downstem, and about an inch of water is the standard example in this record. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Mini Bong works by smoke travels down the downstem and bubbles through water and the inline perc, then rises through the neck to the mouthpiece; the beaker base holds the water and steadies the piece It is made from borosilicate glass body with blue tint, 5 mm wall; glass downstem with inline perc; glass bowl, 14 mm joint, and a common example measures 177.8 mm (7 in) tall; tube 28 mm diameter; beaker base 90 mm diameter, 55 mm tall; water depth 35 mm. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Borosilicate glass body with blue tint, 5 mm wall; glass downstem with inline perc; glass bowl, 14 mm joint

Dimensions: 177.8 mm (7 in) tall; tube 28 mm diameter; beaker base 90 mm diameter, 55 mm tall; water depth 35 mm

Mechanism: Smoke travels down the downstem and bubbles through water and the inline perc, then rises through the neck to the mouthpiece; the beaker base holds the water and steadies the piece

Use: Fill with water to about 35 mm so the downstem slits are submerged, fit the bowl, light and draw slowly, clear the chamber, empty and rinse after use

Care: Empty water after use; rinse with warm water; clean with isopropyl alcohol and coarse salt for residue; dry fully before storage; handle glass gently

Variants: Beaker base with inline perc; straight tube; ice-catcher mini; 5, 6, 7, and 8 inch heights; 10 mm and 14 mm joints

Materials and design

A mini bong is a small glass vessel where the material choice is settled: borosilicate glass, 5 millimetres thick in the standard example, because it resists the thermal shock of a hot bowl joint next to cold water and because it does not change the taste of the smoke. Thin soft glass cracks under the same stress, which is why the sources warn against it at any scale. The beaker base is the defining design choice: its wide foot, 82 millimetres across, holds more water than a straight tube of the same height and lowers the centre of gravity, so a small piece stays planted on a table instead of tipping.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine do-it-yourself build for a glass mini bong: blowing borosilicate to a 5 millimetre wall, grinding a 10 millimetre joint true, and fusing a downstem needs a glass torch, an annealer, and training, so a home-made glass pipe would be unsafe and this record does not pretend otherwise. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling a bought mini bong kit and making the stand it sits on. Buy a six-inch beaker mini bong with a removable downstem and bowl, fit the downstem into the joint so it reaches the water without touching the base, and fit the bowl into the downstem joint, checking that both seal without wobbling.

3D printing

A mini bong itself is not 3D-printable: it is borosilicate glass, and no home printer prints glass, so a printed copy would be plastic, would melt at the bowl joint, and would be unsafe to use. This record says so plainly and gives directions for a printable accessory instead: a base stand and a bowl holder. Print the stand in PETG, which is tough and survives being knocked on a table: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 4 walls, and 40 percent gyroid infill, printed flat on the bed with no supports. The stand is a disc 120 millimetres across with a recess 85 millimetres across and 10 millimetres deep, so the beaker base of the standard six-inch mini bong sits in it and cannot slide.

Use and program

A mini bong is used like a full-size water pipe, only smaller. Fill it with water to about 31.75 millimetres, just enough to submerge the downstem slits by about half an inch, and check the level against the slits: too much water floods the stem and too little leaves the slits exposed. Fit the bowl into the downstem joint, light the bowl, and draw slowly so the smoke bubbles through the water and rises through the neck; the short chamber clears quickly, so one steady draw is enough. Clear the chamber, empty the water after use, and rinse the piece with warm water.

Science proof

A mini bong filters smoke through water in a small chamber, and its physics is the same as a full-size bong with less room for error. Smoke from the bowl travels down the downstem and bubbles through water, which cools it and traps some particles before the smoke rises through the neck. The water depth matters: the sources say just enough to submerge the downstem slits by about half an inch, roughly an inch of water total in most mini bongs, because too much water floods the stem and too little leaves the slits exposed. Borosilicate glass is the standard material because its low thermal expansion resists cracking under the repeated heating of the bowl joint and the cooling of the water chamber, while thin soft glass cracks under the same stress.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula V = pi * (d/2)^2 * h, where V is a chamber volume in cubic millimetres; d is the chamber diameter in millimetres; h is the chamber height in millimetres. The key figures are height_mm = 177.8, tube_diameter_mm = 28.0, base_diameter_mm = 90.0, water_depth_mm = 35.0. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Fill with water to about 35 mm so the downstem slits are submerged, fit the bowl, light and draw slowly, clear the chamber, empty and rinse after use Empty water after use; rinse with warm water; clean with isopropyl alcohol and coarse salt for residue; dry fully before storage; handle glass gently Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

import hashlib, math
def compute():
    height_mm = 177.8; tube_d = 28.0; base_d = 90.0; base_h = 55.0; water_depth = 35.0
    water_vol = math.pi * (base_d / 2.0) ** 2 * water_depth / 1000.0
    base_vol = math.pi * (base_d / 2.0) ** 2 * base_h / 1000.0
    tube_h = height_mm - base_h
    tube_vol = math.pi * (tube_d / 2.0) ** 2 * tube_h / 1000.0
    chamber_vol = base_vol + tube_vol
    water_frac = water_vol / chamber_vol
    return {"height_mm": height_mm, "water_depth_mm": water_depth, "water_volume_ml": round(water_vol, 1), "base_volume_ml": round(base_vol, 1), "tube_volume_ml": round(tube_vol, 1), "chamber_volume_ml": round(chamber_vol, 1), "water_fraction": round(water_frac, 3)}
def main():

    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()

    print(f"base_volume_ml: {a['base_volume_ml']}")
    print(f"tube_volume_ml: {a['tube_volume_ml']}")
    print(f"chamber_volume_ml: {a['chamber_volume_ml']}")
    print(f"water_fraction: {a['water_fraction']}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

history: The mini bong is a full-size water pipe reduced to pocket scale: the same beaker or straight tube, the same downstem and bowl, the same water filtration, in a piece under about eight inches tall. Small water pipes are not new — bubblers and pocket pipes have been sold for decades — but the mini bong as a named type grew with borosilicate glassmaking, which made a thin, heat-resistant tube cheap enough to shrink without cracking. The sources put most mini bongs between four and seven inches tall: four to five inches for the most portable pieces, six to seven inches for a longer smoke path and a larger chamber that is easier to clear. The beaker base became the common form because its wide foot holds more water and keeps a small piece planted on a table, while the straight tube stays the most compact. A six-inch beaker with a 10 or 14 millimetre joint, a removable downstem, and about an inch of water is the standard example in this record. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

materials_design: A mini bong is a small glass vessel where the material choice is settled: borosilicate glass, 5 millimetres thick in the standard example, because it resists the thermal shock of a hot bowl joint next to cold water and because it does not change the taste of the smoke. Thin soft glass cracks under the same stress, which is why the sources warn against it at any scale. The beaker base is the defining design choice: its wide foot, 82 millimetres across, holds more water than a straight tube of the same height and lowers the centre of gravity, so a small piece stays planted on a table instead of tipping. The joint is 10 millimetres in the standard example, with 14 millimetres as the common alternative, and the downstem is removable so it can be cleaned and replaced; the fixed fission downstem on some six-inch beakers diffuses smoke through about 1.25 inches of water. Tolerances are glassblowing tolerances: the joint must be ground true so the bowl seals without wobbling, the downstem must reach the water without touching the base, and the wall thickness must stay even so the piece does not crack at a thin spot. Design varies by form: straight tube for the most compact piece, beaker for stability and water volume, percolator for extra diffusion, ice catcher for a longer cooled path, and silicone for a piece that cannot shatter. The finish is plain polished glass, sometimes with colour in the glass itself, never a coating inside the smoke path.

Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material safely, apply its mechanism cleanly, and survive repeated use without losing its shape. The specification in this record states how the common example meets those three demands, with materials chosen for the job each part does and dimensions that can be measured with a ruler. """Signature Mini Bong — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (mini bong),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for Signature Mini Bong."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        height_mm = 177.8; tube_d = 28.0; base_d = 90.0; base_h = 55.0; water_depth = 35.0
        water_vol = math.pi * (base_d / 2.0) ** 2 * water_depth / 1000.0
        base_vol = math.pi * (base_d / 2.0) ** 2 * base_h / 1000.0
        tube_h = height_mm - base_h
        tube_vol = math.pi * (tube_d / 2.0) ** 2 * tube_h / 1000.0
        chamber_vol = base_vol + tube_vol
        water_frac = water_vol / chamber_vol
        return {"height_mm": height_mm, "water_depth_mm": water_depth, "water_volume_ml": round(water_vol, 1), "base_volume_ml": round(base_vol, 1), "tube_volume_ml": round(tube_vol, 1), "chamber_volume_ml": round(chamber_vol, 1), "water_fraction": round(water_frac, 3)}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

science_proof: A mini bong filters smoke through water in a small chamber, and its physics is the same as a full-size bong with less room for error. Smoke from the bowl travels down the downstem and bubbles through water, which cools it and traps some particles before the smoke rises through the neck. The water depth matters: the sources say just enough to submerge the downstem slits by about half an inch, roughly an inch of water total in most mini bongs, because too much water floods the stem and too little leaves the slits exposed. Borosilicate glass is the standard material because its low thermal expansion resists cracking under the repeated heating of the bowl joint and the cooling of the water chamber, while thin soft glass cracks under the same stress. The beaker base matters for stability: a wide foot lowers the centre of gravity and holds more water than a straight tube of the same height, which is why the demo computes the water volume in the wide base separately from the narrow tube above it. The chamber volume sets the size of a single draw: the smoke path is short, the chamber clears quickly, and the demo checks that the water volume is a sensible fraction of the total chamber, not more than the chamber can hold. History

The grow tent is a portable indoor room: a rigid metal frame wrapped in a reflective fabric skin, with zippered doors, duct ports, and a removable floor tray. It descends from the greenhouse and the photographic darkroom, both enclosed spaces built to control light, and it became a standard smoke-shop and garden product as indoor gardening moved into homes and apartments. Early tents were light canvas over thin poles; the modern form uses powder-coated steel poles, corner connectors, and 600D Oxford fabric lined with reflective Mylar, with 1680D canvas as the premium benchmark. The sizes settled on room footprints: 2 by 2 feet for a closet, 2 by 4 for a small room, 4 by 4 as the common mid-size, and larger footprints up to 10 by 10. The record here describes the product — its frame, its fabric, its ports, its tray — and not how to grow anything inside it. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Grow Tent works by steel frame holds the fabric skin taut; zippered doors close the room; duct ports pass ventilation ducting; diamond-pattern Mylar interior reflects light back into the space It is made from 1680d oxford fabric with diamond-pattern reflective mylar interior; steel poles with steel interlocking pins; steel corner connectors; removable waterproof floor tray, and a common example measures 5 ft x 5 ft footprint, 6.5 ft tall; volume 162.5 cubic feet; floor area 25 square feet; duct ports 6 in and 8 in. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: 1680D Oxford fabric with diamond-pattern reflective Mylar interior; steel poles with steel interlocking pins; steel corner connectors; removable waterproof floor tray

Dimensions: 5 ft x 5 ft footprint, 6.5 ft tall; volume 162.5 cubic feet; floor area 25 square feet; duct ports 6 in and 8 in

Mechanism: Steel frame holds the fabric skin taut; zippered doors close the room; duct ports pass ventilation ducting; diamond-pattern Mylar interior reflects light back into the space

Use: Assemble the frame, pull the fabric skin over it, close the zippers, fit ducting through the ports, hang equipment from the roof bars, lay the floor tray inside

Care: Wipe the Mylar interior with a damp cloth; keep zippers clean and free of grit; dry the tray after spills; check pole connectors and port drawstrings before each setup

Variants: 4x4 ft; 5x5 ft; 4x8 ft; 1680D and 2000D fabric; observation window; extension kits; steel pin frame

Materials and design

A grow tent is a fabric room, and its design is a balance between blocking light, reflecting light, and holding its shape. The skin is 600D Oxford fabric in the standard example, 1680D in the premium version: denier measures the density of the fibres, and higher denier means denser, heavier, more durable fabric that resists pinholes at the seams and blocks outside light better. Inside, the skin is lined with reflective Mylar, rated at 95 percent reflectivity or better, which bounces light back into the space instead of letting the walls absorb it; the premium version uses a diamond-pattern Mylar that spreads the reflected light more evenly.

Build it yourself

A grow tent is a genuine assembly build, and the kit version is designed to be put together by one person with no tools. Unpack the poles and sort them by length: the four vertical poles, the four roof poles, and the four floor poles for a 4 by 4 tent. Push the floor poles into the corner connectors to make the base rectangle, then push the vertical poles into the same connectors and stand the frame up, then fit the roof poles into the top connectors to close the rectangle. Check that every pole is seated fully in its connector and that the frame stands square before the skin goes on.

3D printing

A grow tent itself is not 3D-printable: its skin is 600D Oxford fabric with a Mylar lining and its frame is steel, and no home printer prints fabric or steel poles, so a printed tent would be a model, not a tent. This record says so plainly and gives directions for printable accessories instead: corner connectors and pole clips. Print the corner connectors in PETG, which is tougher than PLA and holds its shape under the load of the frame: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 5 walls, and 60 percent gyroid infill, printed with the socket openings facing up so no supports are needed inside the sockets. Print pole clips in TPU at 0.2 millimetre layers and 30 percent infill, so they grip a pole without cracking.

Use and program

A grow tent is used as an enclosed room for indoor gardening equipment: assemble the frame, pull the skin over it, close the zippers, fit ducting through the ports, hang equipment from the roof bars, and lay the floor tray inside. The tent then does its job as a product: the fabric blocks outside light, the Mylar interior reflects light back into the space, the duct ports pass ventilation ducting, and the tray catches spills. The program in this record computes the numbers behind that use: the tent volume in cubic feet, the floor area, the total fabric area of walls, floor, and ceiling, and the air exchanges per minute that a 402 CFM fan delivers in a 104 cubic foot tent, with the seconds per exchange.

Science proof

A grow tent works as an enclosed reflective room, and its physics is the physics of light and air in a box. The Mylar interior reflects light back toward the centre of the tent instead of letting the walls absorb it, so the same lamp lights the space more evenly; the sources rate good interiors at 95 percent reflectivity or better. The fabric density, measured in denier, sets how well the tent blocks outside light and resists tearing: 600D Oxford cloth is the common mid-range, 1680D is the premium benchmark, and thinner 210D fabric is more prone to pinholes at the seams. The steel frame carries the load: poles and corner connectors hold the fabric taut and support hanging equipment, and the removable floor tray catches spills so the fabric floor stays clean.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula V = L * W * H, where V is the tent volume in cubic feet; L, W, and H are the tent length, width, and height in feet. The key figures are tent_ft = 5 x 5 x 6.5, volume_ft3 = 162.5, fabric_denier = 1680, fan_cfm = 600.0. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Assemble the frame, pull the fabric skin over it, close the zippers, fit ducting through the ports, hang equipment from the roof bars, lay the floor tray inside Wipe the Mylar interior with a damp cloth; keep zippers clean and free of grit; dry the tray after spills; check pole connectors and port drawstrings before each setup Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

Check that every pole is seated fully in its connector and that the frame stands square before the skin goes on. """Demo: grow tent — Signature Grow Tent."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    l_ft = 5.0; w_ft = 5.0; h_ft = 6.5
    volume_ft3 = l_ft * w_ft * h_ft
    floor_ft2 = l_ft * w_ft
    fabric_ft2 = 2 * (l_ft * h_ft + w_ft * h_ft) + 2 * floor_ft2
    fan_cfm = 600.0
    exchanges = fan_cfm / volume_ft3
    seconds_per_exchange = 60.0 / exchanges
    return {"tent_ft": "5 x 5 x 6.5", "volume_ft3": round(volume_ft3, 1), "floor_ft2": round(floor_ft2, 1), "fabric_ft2": round(fabric_ft2, 1), "fan_cfm": fan_cfm, "exchanges_per_min": round(exchanges, 2), "seconds_per_exchange": round(seconds_per_exchange, 1)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    print(f"tent_ft: {a['tent_ft']}")
    print(f"volume_ft3: {a['volume_ft3']}")
    print(f"floor_ft2: {a['floor_ft2']}")
    print(f"fabric_ft2: {a['fabric_ft2']}")
    print(f"fan_cfm: {a['fan_cfm']}")
    print(f"exchanges_per_min: {a['exchanges_per_min']}")
    print(f"seconds_per_exchange: {a['seconds_per_exchange']}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

History

The fabric grow pot is a soft-sided container made of breathable nonwoven fabric, and its history starts with the Smart Pot, which has been made since the 1980s and proved that a porous wall changes how roots behave. Before fabric pots, containers were rigid plastic or clay, and roots reaching the wall would circle it, strangling the plant and starving it of water and nutrients. The fabric pot breaks that pattern: when a root tip reaches the porous wall it meets dry air and stops, and the plant answers by sending out branching roots behind the tip instead. The form spread through garden centres and grow shops in every size from a quarter gallon to a thousand gallons, with 5 gallons the common home size and 7, 10, 15, and 20 gallons for larger plants. Modern pots use needlepunched nonwoven polypropylene in 200 to 500 grams per square metre, double-stitched seams, and sewn handles, and some have square bottoms for stability. The record here describes the pot as a product — its fabric, its capacity, its handles — and not what to plant in it or how to feed anything in it. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Fabric Grow Pot works by porous fabric wall lets air reach the root zone and drains excess water; root tips meeting air stop and branch, preventing circling roots It is made from 500 gsm needlepunched nonwoven polypropylene fabric; bonded polyester thread, quad-stitched; reinforced webbing handles, and a common example measures 7 gallon (26.5 l) nominal; 33 cm diameter x 30 cm tall; two reinforced handles. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: 500 GSM needlepunched nonwoven polypropylene fabric; bonded polyester thread, quad-stitched; reinforced webbing handles

Dimensions: 7 gallon (26.5 L) nominal; 33 cm diameter x 30 cm tall; two reinforced handles

Mechanism: Porous fabric wall lets air reach the root zone and drains excess water; root tips meeting air stop and branch, preventing circling roots

Use: Set the pot on a tray, fill with growing mix, place it where it will stay, lift by both handles when moving it

Care: Empty after use, brush off dried mix, rinse with water and dry fully before storage; check seams and handles for wear; fold flat for storage

Variants: 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, and 20 gallon; reinforced handles; square bottom; black fabric; 500 GSM

Materials and design

A fabric grow pot is a container made of cloth, and its design is the fabric itself. The standard example uses 300 grams per square metre needlepunched nonwoven polypropylene: needlepunching tangles the fibres into a felt that holds together without weaving, and the nonwoven structure leaves pores through the whole wall so air and water pass through. Budget pots sit near 200 to 250 GSM and premium pots reach 500 GSM; thicker fabric holds its shape better, resists tearing at the handles, and lasts more seasons, while thinner fabric dries faster and costs less. The seams are the weak point, so they are double-stitched with bonded polyester thread, which resists rot and constant moisture better than cotton thread, and the premium version is quad-stitched.

Build it yourself

A fabric grow pot is a genuine sewing build, and it can be made with nonwoven polypropylene fabric, a sewing machine, and bonded polyester thread. Cut a rectangle of 300 GSM nonwoven polypropylene 96 centimetres long and 26 centimetres tall for a 5-gallon pot, and cut a circle 31 centimetres across for the base. Fold the rectangle into a cylinder with the long edges overlapping by 1 centimetre, pin it, and sew the side seam twice with a straight stitch, keeping the stitch 5 millimetres from the edge. Pin the base circle to the bottom edge of the cylinder, easing the fabric around the curve, and sew it twice around the full circle, then turn the pot right side out and check that the base sits flat.

3D printing

A fabric grow pot itself is not 3D-printable: it is nonwoven polypropylene fabric, and no home printer prints a porous fabric wall, so a printed pot would be a rigid plastic tub, not a fabric pot, and would lose the air pruning that is the whole point. This record says so plainly and gives directions for printable accessories instead: rim clips and a saucer. Print the rim clips in PETG, which is tough and survives being handled with wet hands: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 3 walls, and 30 percent gyroid infill, printed flat on the bed with no supports. The clips are C-shaped, 40 millimetres long, and snap over the rim of the pot to hold a label tag or a support stake.

Use and program

A fabric grow pot is used as a container: set it on a tray or saucer, fill it with growing mix, place it where it will stay, and lift it by both handles when it needs moving. The porous wall then does its job as a product: air reaches the root zone through the fabric, excess water drains through the wall instead of pooling, and root tips that reach the wall meet air and branch instead of circling. The program in this record computes the numbers behind that use: the pot volume in litres and gallons from its diameter and height, the fabric surface area of the side wall and base, and the mass of the growing mix it holds at a density of 0.45 grams per cubic centimetre.

Science proof

The fabric grow pot works by air pruning, and the mechanism is simple enough to state in one sentence: a root tip that reaches air stops growing and branches instead. In a rigid plastic pot the root hits a solid wall, turns, and circles the container, and the circling mass chokes water and nutrient uptake. In a fabric pot the wall is porous nonwoven polypropylene, so air passes through the fabric and dries the root tip on contact, which triggers lateral branching and a dense fibrous root mass with far more root ends — the sources report up to 200 percent more root ends than rigid containers. The same porosity gives superior drainage: excess water passes through the fabric instead of pooling at the bottom, and the sources quote water passing at 50 to 150 litres per square metre per second through the nonwoven wall.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula V = pi * (d/2)^2 * h, where V is the pot volume in cubic centimetres; d is the pot diameter in centimetres; h is the pot height in centimetres. The key figures are diameter_cm = 33.0, height_cm = 30.0, volume_L = 25.64, fabric_gsm = 500. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Set the pot on a tray, fill with growing mix, place it where it will stay, lift by both handles when moving it Empty after use, brush off dried mix, rinse with water and dry fully before storage; check seams and handles for wear; fold flat for storage Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

Legal note

"""Demo: fabric grow pot — Signature Fabric Grow Pot."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    d_cm = 33.0; h_cm = 30.0; density = 0.45
    vol_cm3 = math.pi * (d_cm / 2.0) ** 2 * h_cm
    vol_L = vol_cm3 / 1000.0
    vol_gal = vol_L / 3.78541
    side_area = math.pi * d_cm * h_cm
    bottom_area = math.pi * (d_cm / 2.0) ** 2

    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()

    print(f"diameter_cm: {a['diameter_cm']}")
    print(f"height_cm: {a['height_cm']}")
    print(f"volume_L: {a['volume_L']}")
    print(f"volume_gal: {a['volume_gal']}")
    print(f"fabric_area_cm2: {a['fabric_area_cm2']}")
    print(f"mix_mass_kg: {a['mix_mass_kg']}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

In a rigid plastic pot the root hits a solid wall, turns, and circles the container, and the circling mass chokes water and nutrient uptake. History

The inline duct fan is a cylindrical fan that sits inside a run of ducting and pulls air through an enclosed path, and it became the standard ventilation tool for grow tents as indoor gardening grew. Earlier ventilation used axial fans that blew air around an open room; the inline fan instead mounts in the duct itself, so it can exhaust stale air from a tent through a carbon filter and out of the room. The common sizes are 4, 6, 8, and 10 inches of duct diameter, with the 4-inch fan moving about 190 to 210 CFM for a 2 by 2 or 2 by 4 tent and the 6-inch fan moving about 390 to 440 CFM for a 4 by 4 tent. Modern fans use EC motors with speed controllers and temperature and humidity sensors, and the best-known lines, such as the AC Infinity CLOUDLINE series, publish 205 CFM at 28 dBA for the 4-inch model and 402 CFM at 32 dBA for the 6-inch model. The record here describes the fan as a product — its size, its airflow, its power, its noise — and not how to grow anything in the space it ventilates. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Inline Duct Fan works by eC motor spins an impeller inside the duct, pulling air through the enclosed path; smart controller sets the airflow from temperature and humidity readings; mounted high in the tent, it exhausts warm humid air first It is made from steel housing; steel mounting brackets; ec motor with smart controller; aluminium impeller; temperature and humidity sensor, and a common example measures 8 in (203.2 mm) duct diameter; housing about 340 mm long; rated 807 cfm; 34 dba at full speed; 60 w. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Steel housing; steel mounting brackets; EC motor with smart controller; aluminium impeller; temperature and humidity sensor

Dimensions: 8 in (203.2 mm) duct diameter; housing about 340 mm long; rated 807 CFM; 34 dBA at full speed; 60 W

Mechanism: EC motor spins an impeller inside the duct, pulling air through the enclosed path; smart controller sets the airflow from temperature and humidity readings; mounted high in the tent, it exhausts warm humid air first

Use: Mount the fan in the duct run with clamps, connect ducting to a carbon filter on the intake side, set the speed on the controller, check that air flows out of the tent

Care: Switch off before cleaning; wipe the housing and impeller blades; check duct clamps and cords; keep the intake clear of loose fabric

Variants: 6 in 402 CFM; 8 in 807 CFM; 10 in 1200 CFM; smart controller; temperature and humidity sensor

Materials and design

An inline duct fan is a small machine built around one job: moving a known volume of air through a duct at a known noise level. The housing is ABS plastic in the standard example and steel in the premium version: ABS is light, cheap, and quiet, while steel is heavier and survives knocks in a workshop. Inside, an EC motor spins an aluminium impeller; EC motors are chosen because they hold their speed under load, run quietly at part speed, and draw less power than older AC motors when turned down. The impeller blades are curved to push air along the duct rather than churn it, and the housing is a smooth cylinder so the air path has no sharp edges to whistle.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine do-it-yourself build for an inline duct fan: winding an EC motor, balancing an impeller, and rating a fan at 402 CFM needs a factory and test equipment, so a home-made fan would be a rough imitation that moves far less air than its label claims. This record says so plainly and gives the closest genuine maker activity instead: assembling a duct run and mounting a bought fan in it. Measure the run from the tent port to the outside, cut flexible ducting to length with a little slack, and fit a hose clamp over each end. Mount the fan high in the tent, because warm humid air rises, using the steel mounting brackets and screws, and check that the airflow arrow on the housing points out of the tent.

3D printing

The inline duct fan itself is not 3D-printable as a working fan: its EC motor and balanced impeller cannot be printed, and a printed impeller would spin out of balance and fail. This record says so plainly and gives directions for printable accessories instead: a duct adapter and a mounting bracket. Print the duct adapter in PETG, which is tough and holds its shape in warm air: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 4 walls, and 40 percent gyroid infill, printed upright with the bore vertical so no supports are needed inside the bore. The adapter steps a 6-inch duct down to a 4-inch duct, with a 20 millimetre straight section at each end for the hose clamps.

Use and program

An inline duct fan is used by mounting it in a duct run and setting its speed. Mount the fan high in the tent with its airflow arrow pointing out of the tent, connect ducting to the carbon filter on the intake side, tighten the clamps, and set the speed on the controller so the tent holds a slight negative pressure — the walls pull in gently — which shows that air is being drawn out faster than it leaks in.

Science proof

An inline duct fan moves air by volume, and its sizing rule is the volume rule: measure the space in cubic feet and choose a fan that can exchange that volume about once per minute, then add a margin for real-world losses. A carbon filter on the intake typically cuts effective airflow by roughly 20 to 25 percent, so the sources add a 25 percent buffer to the bare volume figure; a 4 by 4 by 8 foot tent is 128 cubic feet and needs a fan rated for at least about 160 CFM once the filter is counted. The fan in this record is a 6-inch unit rated at 402 CFM, which exchanges a 104 cubic foot tent nearly four times per minute at full speed and can therefore run well below full speed for quieter operation.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula v = Q / A, where v is the air velocity in metres per second; Q is the airflow in cubic metres per second; A is the duct cross-section in square metres. The key figures are duct_diameter_in = 8.0, airflow_cfm = 807.0, power_w = 60.0, noise_dba = 34. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Mount the fan in the duct run with clamps, connect ducting to a carbon filter on the intake side, set the speed on the controller, check that air flows out of the tent Switch off before cleaning; wipe the housing and impeller blades; check duct clamps and cords; keep the intake clear of loose fabric Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

Legal note

History

The carbon filter is a canister of activated carbon that scrubs odour from exhaust air, and it became a standard grow-tent part once indoor gardening moved into shared buildings. Activated carbon has been used to purify air and water for more than a century: its surface is full of microscopic pores, and gas molecules stick to those pores by adsorption, a surface effect, not absorption into the material. The grow-tent form is a steel canister with a flange on one end, a bed of carbon held between two mesh cylinders, and a cloth pre-filter sleeve that catches dust before it reaches the carbon. Common sizes match the common fans: 4 inches by 12 inches for a 2 by 2 or 2 by 4 tent, 6 inches by 16 inches for a 4 by 4 tent, with a bed about 38 millimetres thick of virgin Australian carbon rated at 1200 or higher iodine value. Lifespans vary by use: makers quote 3 to 6 months for heavy use and up to 18 months of continuous use for thick-bed canisters, and the honest rule is to replace the carbon when odour starts to leak. The record here describes the filter as a product — its canister, its carbon bed, its airflow, its lifespan — and not how to grow anything in the space it serves. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Carbon Filter works by fan pulls air through the outer mesh, across the activated carbon bed where odour molecules adsorb to the carbon pores, and out through the flange to the duct It is made from stainless-steel canister and flange; virgin australian activated carbon, 1200+ iodine value; stainless mesh cylinders; washable cloth pre-filter sleeve, and a common example measures 6 in (150 mm) flange; canister 150 mm diameter x 400 mm long; carbon bed 38 mm thick; rated about 402 cfm. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Stainless-steel canister and flange; virgin Australian activated carbon, 1200+ iodine value; stainless mesh cylinders; washable cloth pre-filter sleeve

Dimensions: 6 in (150 mm) flange; canister 150 mm diameter x 400 mm long; carbon bed 38 mm thick; rated about 402 CFM

Mechanism: Fan pulls air through the outer mesh, across the activated carbon bed where odour molecules adsorb to the carbon pores, and out through the flange to the duct

Use: Hang the canister inside the tent on straps, fit the pre-filter sleeve, connect the flange to the inline fan with ducting and clamps, run the fan so air passes through the bed

Care: Wash or replace the pre-filter sleeve regularly; keep the canister dry; replace the carbon or the canister when odour leaks; store in a dry place

Variants: 4 in x 12 in; 6 in x 16 in; 8 in x 24 in; refillable canisters; reversible flange; 38 mm and 52 mm beds

Materials and design

A carbon filter is a steel canister built around a bed of carbon, and every part of its design serves the airflow through that bed. The canister is galvanised steel in the standard example and stainless steel in the premium version: galvanised steel resists rust and corrosion at a low price, while stainless steel lasts longer in damp air. Inside, the carbon bed is held between two mesh cylinders, an outer mesh and an inner mesh, so air must cross the full 38 millimetre bed to get from the outside to the flange; the bed thickness is the key number, because a thicker bed gives the air a longer dwell time and adsorbs more, and 52 millimetre beds exist for heavier use.

Build it yourself

A carbon filter is a genuine maker build in its refillable form, and the sources describe a jar-based version that works on the same principle as the bought canister. Take a mesh canister or a large jar with holes drilled through its walls, and fill it with activated carbon — aquarium-grade granules work — to within a half inch of the rim, so the bed is deep and even. Fit a cloth pre-filter sleeve over the outside to catch dust before it reaches the carbon, and fit a flange or a duct adapter to one end so the canister connects to the inline fan with a hose clamp.

3D printing

A carbon filter itself is not 3D-printable: its canister is steel, its bed is activated carbon, and no home printer prints either, so a printed filter would be a plastic tube with no carbon in it and would scrub nothing. This record says so plainly and gives directions for printable accessories instead: a flange adapter and a pre-filter frame. Print the flange adapter in PETG, which is tough and holds its shape in warm air: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 4 walls, and 40 percent gyroid infill, printed upright with the bore vertical so no supports are needed inside the bore. The adapter steps a 4-inch filter flange up to a 6-inch duct, with a 20 millimetre straight section at each end for the hose clamps.

Use and program

A carbon filter is used by hanging it in the exhaust path and letting the fan pull air through it. Hang the canister inside the tent on straps, fit the pre-filter sleeve over it, connect the flange to the inline fan with ducting and clamps, and run the fan so air passes from the tent through the carbon bed and out through the duct; the filter cleans the air on its way out of the tent, which is an odour problem, not an air-quality problem for anything inside.

Science proof

A carbon filter works by adsorption: air passes through a bed of activated carbon, and odour molecules stick to the enormous internal surface of the carbon pores instead of passing through. The bed in this record is 38 millimetres thick, the common RC412 grade of virgin Australian carbon rated at 1200 or higher iodine value, which is a measure of how much the carbon can adsorb. The canister is an annulus: air enters through the outer mesh, crosses the 38 millimetre bed, and leaves through the inner mesh to the fan, so the carbon volume is the volume between the outer and inner cylinders, about 2.22 litres in the 4-inch by 12-inch example.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula V = pi * (R^2 - r^2) * L, where V is the carbon bed volume in cubic millimetres; R is the outer radius in millimetres; r is the inner radius in millimetres; L is the canister length in millimetres. The key figures are outer_diameter_mm = 150.0, length_mm = 400.0, bed_mm = 38.0, airflow_cfm = 402.0, lifespan_months = 6.0. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Hang the canister inside the tent on straps, fit the pre-filter sleeve, connect the flange to the inline fan with ducting and clamps, run the fan so air passes through the bed Wash or replace the pre-filter sleeve regularly; keep the canister dry; replace the carbon or the canister when odour leaks; store in a dry place Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

Fit a cloth pre-filter sleeve over the outside to catch dust before it reaches the carbon, and fit a flange or a duct adapter to one end so the canister connects to the inline fan with a hose clamp. Mount the canister inside the tent on straps, connect it to the fan, and run the fan so air is pulled through the bed; the sources note that a jar-based build suits tents up to 3 by 3 feet and works best with a 4-inch fan, while a 4 by 4 tent needs a bought canister with a proportionally larger bed. For a bought canister, the genuine maker task is refilling it: open the end cap, pour out the spent carbon, refill with fresh virgin activated carbon to the same depth, and close the cap tightly so no air bypasses the bed. Replace the carbon when odour starts to leak, and keep the pre-filter clean, because a clean pre-filter is the cheapest way to extend the bed life. Never reuse spent carbon: once its pores are full it adsorbs nothing more.

"""Demo: carbon filter — Signature Carbon Filter."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    outer_d = 150.0; length = 400.0; bed_mm = 38.0; cfm = 402.0; months = 6.0
    outer_r = outer_d / 2.0; inner_r = outer_r - bed_mm
    carbon_vol = math.pi * (outer_r ** 2 - inner_r ** 2) * length / 1000000.0
    outer_area = math.pi * outer_d * length / 1000000.0
    flow_m3s = cfm * 0.000471947
    face_vel = flow_m3s / outer_area
    hours = months * 30.0 * 24.0
    return {"outer_diameter_mm": outer_d, "length_mm": length, "bed_mm": bed_mm, "carbon_volume_L": round(carbon_vol, 2), "outer_area_m2": round(outer_area, 4), "face_velocity_ms": round(face_vel, 2), "lifespan_months": months, "lifespan_hours": round(hours, 0)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    print(f"outer_diameter_mm: {a['outer_diameter_mm']}")
    print(f"length_mm: {a['length_mm']}")
    print(f"bed_mm: {a['bed_mm']}")
    print(f"carbon_volume_L: {a['carbon_volume_L']}")
    print(f"outer_area_m2: {a['outer_area_m2']}")
    print(f"face_velocity_ms: {a['face_velocity_ms']}")
    print(f"lifespan_months: {a['lifespan_months']}")
    print(f"lifespan_hours: {a['lifespan_hours']}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

body:
History

The drying rack is a hanging tower of mesh tiers that holds plant material in the air so it can dry evenly, and it descends from the herb-drying frames and net bags that gardeners have used for centuries. The modern form is a collapsible cylinder of polyester mesh over a flexible steel wireframe, with zippered chambers stacked one above another and a hook at the top so the whole tower hangs from a bar. The standard example in this record is the six-tier rack, 600 millimetres across and 1,194 millimetres long when hanging, with each chamber 171 millimetres high; a four-tier version, 457 millimetres across, fits a 2 by 2 tent, and eight-tier versions reach 1,700 millimetres. The rack collapses flat into a carry bag when the season is over, and it springs open from the bag in seconds. The record here describes the rack as a product — its tiers, its mesh, its frame, its hook — and it does not tell anyone how to dry any particular plant or how long any drying or curing should take. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

Signature Drying Rack works by material is spread in a single layer on each mesh tier; air passes through the mesh floor and walls; the tower hangs from one hook so air moves around it on all sides It is made from non-toxic polyester mesh, heavy grade; stainless-steel wireframe; steel hanging hook with swivel; zippered chambers; carry bag, and a common example measures 8 tiers; 600 mm (24 in) diameter; 1,700 mm hanging length; each chamber 170 mm high. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

This Signature design is a design study: a new design for the same supply type, described in full and never presented as a real product or as established fact.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Non-toxic polyester mesh, heavy grade; stainless-steel wireframe; steel hanging hook with swivel; zippered chambers; carry bag

Dimensions: 8 tiers; 600 mm (24 in) diameter; 1,700 mm hanging length; each chamber 170 mm high

Mechanism: Material is spread in a single layer on each mesh tier; air passes through the mesh floor and walls; the tower hangs from one hook so air moves around it on all sides

Use: Hang the rack from a bar or hook, open the zipper of a tier, spread material in a single layer, close the zipper, repeat for the other tiers

Care: Empty each tier after use; brush off loose material; wash the mesh gently and dry fully; collapse flat into the carry bag for storage

Variants: 4, 6, and 8 tiers; 600 mm (24 in) and 800 mm (32 in) diameters; removable tiers; swivel hook; with carry bag

Materials and design

A drying rack is a tower of mesh and wire, and its design is a balance between holding a load and folding flat. The mesh is non-toxic polyester, chosen because it is breathable, washable, and strong enough to hold material without stretching, and because it lets air pass through the floor of each tier as well as around the sides. The frame is flexible steel wire, chosen because it holds each disc open under load and still folds flat into a carry bag when the season is over; the sources describe the wire as rust-proof and high-tensile.

Build it yourself

A drying rack is a genuine woodworking and sewing build, and it can be made from dowels, mesh, and cord. Cut six discs of polyester mesh 600 millimetres across, and cut six wooden rings from 12 millimetre dowel bent into circles 600 millimetres across, or use ready-made embroidery hoops of the same size as the rings. Sew each mesh disc to its ring with a whip stitch around the full circle, pulling the mesh taut so it does not sag in the middle. Cut three lengths of cord 1,400 millimetres long, and tie them to the rings at three points spaced evenly around the circle, spacing the rings 171 millimetres apart along the cords so the chambers match the standard rack.

3D printing

A drying rack itself is not 3D-printable: its tiers are polyester mesh and its frame is steel wire, and no home printer prints mesh or wire, so a printed rack would be a solid plastic disc with no airflow and would not dry anything. This record says so plainly and gives directions for printable accessories instead: tier clips and a hook adapter. Print the tier clips in PETG, which is tough and survives being handled with wet hands: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 3 walls, and 30 percent gyroid infill, printed flat on the bed with no supports. The clips are C-shaped, 50 millimetres long, and snap over the wireframe ring to hold a label tag or to join two tiers together.

Use and program

A drying rack is used by hanging it and filling its tiers. Hang the rack from a bar or hook, open the zipper of a tier, spread material in a single layer on the mesh, close the zipper, and repeat for the other tiers; the tower then hangs clear of the floor with air moving around it on all sides and through the mesh floors. The program in this record computes the numbers behind that use: the area of one 600 millimetre tier, the total area across all six tiers, the volume of one chamber at 171 millimetres high, the total volume of the tower, and the load capacity per tier from the stated 3 kilogram total.

Science proof

A drying rack works by giving air access to material from every direction at once. Each tier is a flat disc of open mesh, so air passes through the floor of the chamber as well as around its sides, and the material is spread in a single layer instead of piled in a heap where the middle stays damp. The mesh is non-toxic polyester, chosen because it is breathable, washable, and strong enough to hold a load without stretching, and the frame is flexible steel wire, chosen because it holds the disc open under load and still folds flat for storage. The numbers show the scale: one tier of the six-tier rack is 600 millimetres across, giving about 0.28 square metres of drying area per tier and about 1.70 square metres across all six, with each chamber about 171 millimetres high and about 48 litres of space.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula A = pi * (d/2)^2, where A is one tier area in square millimetres; d is the tier diameter in millimetres. The key figures are tiers = 8, diameter_mm = 600.0, chamber_height_mm = 170.0, hanging_length_mm = 1700.0, capacity_kg = 4.0. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Hang the rack from a bar or hook, open the zipper of a tier, spread material in a single layer, close the zipper, repeat for the other tiers Empty each tier after use; brush off loose material; wash the mesh gently and dry fully; collapse flat into the carry bag for storage Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

Legal note

"""Demo: drying rack — Signature Drying Rack."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    tiers = 8; d_mm = 600.0; chamber_h = 170.0; length_mm = 1700.0; capacity_kg = 4.0
    tier_area = math.pi * (d_mm / 2.0) ** 2 / 1000000.0
    total_area = tier_area * tiers
    tier_vol = tier_area * (chamber_h / 1000.0) * 1000.0
    total_vol = tier_vol * tiers
    per_tier_kg = capacity_kg / tiers
    return {"tiers": tiers, "diameter_mm": d_mm, "chamber_height_mm": chamber_h, "hanging_length_mm": length_mm, "tier_area_m2": round(tier_area, 4), "total_area_m2": round(total_area, 3), "tier_volume_L": round(tier_vol, 1), "total_volume_L": round(total_vol, 1), "capacity_kg": capacity_kg, "per_tier_kg": round(per_tier_kg, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    print(f"tiers: {a['tiers']}")
    print(f"diameter_mm: {a['diameter_mm']}")
    print(f"chamber_height_mm: {a['chamber_height_mm']}")
    print(f"hanging_length_mm: {a['hanging_length_mm']}")
    print(f"tier_area_m2: {a['tier_area_m2']}")
    print(f"total_area_m2: {a['total_area_m2']}")
    print(f"tier_volume_L: {a['tier_volume_L']}")
    print(f"total_volume_L: {a['total_volume_L']}")
    print(f"capacity_kg: {a['capacity_kg']}")
    print(f"per_tier_kg: {a['per_tier_kg']}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
